content.content:
=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.

 ## How he wants to be spoken to

**What was tried.** The plan in `reviews/template-checking-plan.md` says the compiler cannot type-check grammar extensions because template gaps trip it up. A template gap is the placeholder inside a grammar rule's transformer body, the part that gets filled in with the user's parsed expression. The plan proposed four small edits to the compiler, 31 changed lines in total.

**How it was tried without unsealing.** The worker copied the four files, edited the copies, compiled them separately, and put the compiled classes ahead of the real ones on the classpath. Java takes the first class it finds, so the edited copies win and no tracked file changes. For the full test suite the compiled classes were copied over the build directory temporarily, then the originals were put back and verified by checksum.

**What the result was.** The full test suite stays green with the edits in place, 1,377 plus 382 tests, zero failures. The seven grammar test programs that the interpreter runs today also compile and run on the compiler path, printing the same output. So the ledger row that says "grammar extensions do not compile" is fixed by these four edits.

**One thing still fails.** Parentheses inside a template, like `(a + b) * c`, are lost once the grammar comes from the cache on disk. The compiler saves analysed grammar files as cache files and reloads them later. The code that writes those files only writes the fields declared on the gap class itself. The "was parenthesized" flag lives on the parent class, so it is never written and never read back. A fifth edit, in the reflection-based writer, makes it write inherited fields too. That edit works in a direct test but was not run through the full suite.

**Two things the plan got wrong.** The plan blamed the parser for losing the parentheses. The parser keeps them; the type checker reads the flag one phase later. The edits are the same either way. Second, the plan wanted the syntax-abstraction JUnit tests as a gate. Those tests are broken as shipped, 14 of 17 fail before and after the edits, and the build already leaves them out of testFast. They cannot be a gate.

Yes, it makes sense. Here is what I hear you asking, part by part, then answers to the two direct questions, then how I would produce it.

**What you are asking for.** One document, a map of the territory, written before the sealed tree is opened. It has these parts:

1. **Repository architecture.** The modules in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` and the top-level directories, each with its role and what it depends on. The repo already has a partial version of this in `explorations/repo-internals.md`; the map either extends it or supersedes it.
2. **Language architecture, spec to implementation.** For each feature area of the latest committed spec (not the 1.0 frozen one), where it lives: in the parser, in the static checker, in the interpreter, in the compiler, in the shipped library, or nowhere. The particular question you named: what enables the numeric tower. The tower is library code, but it stands on traits, generic types, operator overloading and dispatch, and those are language mechanisms implemented in the checker and runtime. The map separates enabling blocks from things built on them.
3. **The compile pipeline, phase by phase.** Rats! parser produces the AST; grammar extensions are expanded; desugaring; type checking; bytecode generation with ASM; the runtime class loader that generates code on the fly; the Java interop surface. For each phase: which module, what it produces, what the next phase needs from it. You are right that there is Java interop, the `nativeHelpers` module and the compiler's `NativeHelper` bindings are that surface.
4. **Test coverage.** Which test directories exercise which layer, whether the interpreter and compiler suites are shared or separate, and how much of each layer has no test at all. This decides how safely each layer can be modified.
5. **Gaps on the path.** Of the 309 ledger rows, which ones sit on the road from today's tree to a fast compiled microgpt, in dependency order, and what breaks if each is left alone.
6. **The development loop.** What makes an iteration slow, which of those costs are ledger rows already, and which are tooling.
7. **A dependency map.** Touching this affects that, so that fixes are ordered and the artifact does not fall apart under edits.

**The guiding constraint you stated.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest spec, not redesign the language. The measuring stick is one program: microgpt compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microgpt later gives the floor to aim at.

**The phase boundary you described.** Tag the tree at the unsealing point, then start the next phase: modifying the original sources, with lessons from the explorations. The map is the last prep before that tag.

**Terminology: gate.** A gate is the check a change must pass before it is accepted. Ours has been the fully green suite: `ant testFast` plus `ant testSystem`. The map's coverage part tells us where that gate is blind.

**Fortify and Fortick, answered.** Fortify is an Emacs Lisp program, `Fortify/fortify.el`, 8,024 lines, plus a LaTeX style file. It rewrites Fortress source into LaTeX commands so the spec and papers show code as typeset math. It runs from `bin/fortify` or an Ant task. Fortick is a wrapper script that takes a document with backtick-delimited Fortress snippets and replaces them with the fortified form. Neither touches the language, parser, or runtime. The separate `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. We would touch Fortify only if we changed the spec's LaTeX build or wanted the microgpt article typeset that way. Given your verdict on the notation, that is a no. Your verdict itself I record as a position: the 2D rendering is presentation, not language, and not on our path.

**One correction to your picture.** The Unicode operators and mathematical spelling are in the language itself. Fortress source can be written with `∑`, `∈`, `×` and juxtaposition directly, and the ASCII spellings are aliases the parser accepts. Fortify only adds the typesetting on top. So dropping Fortify loses nothing on our path.

**How I would produce the map.** Survey work goes to Opus workers, one brief per part where it needs reading of code or counting of tests: the module and phase walk (parts 1 and 3), the spec-to-implementation table (part 2), and the test coverage census (part 4). Parts 5 to 7 are design and stay in this thread, built on the ledger and the three survey reports. The map lives in `explorations/coordinator/` beside FACTS and POSITIONS, since it is the thing read at every session start from the next phase on.

On your word, the three survey workers start.

5:**Fortify renders written source, not a mathematical view selected by an object's type or value.** A library can expose both matrix multiplication and indexed access on the same object. The programmer chooses which expression to write; the library supplies its meaning; Fortify supplies a spatial rendering of its spelling. Those mechanisms cooperate, but none substitutes for the others.
20:![Actual Fortify rendering of the two expressions](figures/same-data.png)
39:![Actual Fortify rendering: an unequal pair looks like the same subscripted symbol](figures/subscript-meaning.png)
41:The first assertion passes: **`x_i` is a named scalar, 123; `x[i]` accesses the vector's second element, 6.** Fortify renders both as the same subscripted symbol. The picture therefore appears to assert that a quantity differs from itself. This is a concrete failure of an unqualified “the picture is the mathematics” criterion: the reader also needs a notation convention that prevents these collisions.
43:The second assertion passes too. Tight `A[0,1]` renders as a subscript; the space in `A[0, 1]` makes Fortify retain the brackets. In this particular access, changing that space changes presentation without changing the evaluated value. This is not a general claim that whitespace is semantically irrelevant in Fortress.
45:The initial spelling `x_1` was rejected by the interpreter at line 14. Its [source](evidence/attempt-01.fss.txt), [output](evidence/attempt-01.out.txt), and [record](evidence/attempt-01.json) are preserved. The successful version uses `x_i`. Fortify had already processed the rejected spelling into TeX: successful typesetting is not a parser or execution test. We have not classified the rejected spelling against the specification or added a new gap-ledger entry for it.
47:## Where the presentation is controlled
49:The inspected path is [bin/fortick](../../bin/fortick) → [Fortify/fortify.el](../../Fortify/fortify.el) → TeX using [fortify.sty](../../Fortify/fortify.sty). The Emacs implementation tokenizes, repairs tokens, performs a lightweight error-correcting structural parse, recognizes idioms, and manages spacing. It does not use the interpreter's values or the compiler's inferred types. See also [fortify-doc.txt](../../Fortify/fortify-doc.txt).
51:| Written construct | Semantic mechanism | Presentation mechanism in Fortify |
61:The library already supplies `.t()`; later experiments define postfix transpose notation around it. Ledger claim **64** records a working custom postfix operator, while **84** records a dotted-receiver spelling trap. Type parameters and dimension annotations may themselves render mathematically, but Fortify renders what was written rather than deriving those annotations.
63:Runtime printing through `asString` is another facility. It should not be confused with this source-to-TeX pipeline. Likewise, the new [APL exploration](../apl-probes/REPORT.md) demonstrates syntax extensions that expand into executable Fortress structure. Whether each custom syntax has an adequate Fortify presentation needs its own check; the inspected renderer does not automatically consume those grammar definitions.
109:Use **one existing kernel, row-wise RMS normalization**, to compare the Run B and B2 formulations. Keep the independent mathematical definition fixed. For each candidate, record its carrier, shape convention, inherited operations, pullback representation, and numerical/effect obligations; then compare exact source and actual Fortify rendering. The existing review includes a diagonal-scaling alternative, so do not rediscover or silently discard it: account for its extra matrix work.

"""tlib: the curator's messages, and the coordinating session's message that each one answered,
read along the transcript's reply chain (standard library).

His messages are exactly what explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py's load() gives: the

and the copy until 2026-10-08T15-41 included) and the first session on the `transcripts` branch;
deduplicated by uuid; queued messages with the time he sent them. load_msgs() rebuilds that list
from a per-file index (cache below) with show.py's own functions, in show.py's file order, so the
list is the same; tests.py checks it against show.load().

The message he answered (Talk.answered) follows the chain of the transcript itself: each line's
parentUuid (a compaction's logicalParentUuid), back from his message. Every line on the chain is
one of:
  his     a message of his (show.py's test), or his message queued while a turn ran, delivered
          into that turn (a queued_command attachment that is not a notification)
  text    an assistant line of the session (not a sidechain) holding text
  note    a prompt that is not his: Stop-hook feedback, an agent's message or hand-back, a task

          you left off", a worker restart notice, a skill's text, an image, a local command)
Going back from his message, the texts met are collected; reaching a note drops them as a turn
not to him (they are listed as skipped), and reaching a prompt of his makes them the answer: the

older question. Two checks on the rule: a skipped turn that answers a notification and ends with
